signal.title: BIST 100
signal.standing: The 100 largest companies on Borsa İstanbul, Türkiye's only stock exchange. It is priced in lira, so its level carries the country's inflation as much as its earnings: read the direction, not the number.

signal.title: Ibovespa
signal.standing: The Índice Bovespa tracks the most traded shares on B3, the São Paulo exchange that is Brazil's only stock market and Latin America's largest. Iron ore, oil and Brazilian interest rates drive it.

signal.title: CAC 40
signal.standing: The 40 largest companies listed on Euronext Paris, France's main stock market. Luxury goods and energy dominate it, which leaves the index unusually exposed to Chinese consumer demand.

signal.title: TA-125
signal.standing: The 125 largest companies by market value on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, Israel's only stock market. It trades Sunday to Thursday and is heavily weighted to banks, defence and technology.

signal.title: SMI
signal.standing: The Swiss Market Index: the 20 largest companies on the SIX Swiss Exchange in Zurich, Switzerland's main market. Nestlé, Roche and Novartis carry it, which makes it defensive when the world turns risk-off.

signal.title: OMXS30
signal.standing: The OMX Stockholm 30: the 30 most traded shares on Nasdaq Stockholm, Sweden's main stock exchange. Nordic industrials and telecoms dominate it, which makes it a useful early read on European capital spending.

signal.title: DAX
signal.standing: Frankfurt's benchmark index, tracking the 40 largest companies listed on the Deutsche Börse. Carmakers, chemicals and industrial engineering dominate it, and roughly three-quarters of their revenue is earned outside Germany.

signal.title: Hang Seng
signal.standing: The Hang Seng Index tracks the largest, most traded companies on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. It is where mainland Chinese companies meet foreign capital, and the clearest daily read on sentiment toward China.

signal.title: FTSE 100
signal.standing: The Financial Times Stock Exchange 100: the 100 largest companies on the London Stock Exchange by market value. Most of their revenue is earned abroad, so a falling pound tends to push the index up.

signal.title: S&P/TSX Composite
signal.standing: The broad benchmark of the Toronto Stock Exchange, Canada's main market, tracking its largest listed companies. Energy producers, miners and banks dominate it, so it moves with commodity prices as much as with corporate profits.

signal.title: S&P 500
signal.standing: An index of 500 large companies listed on US stock exchanges, weighted by market value. It is the benchmark most pension and index funds are measured against, and a handful of technology firms carry much of its weight.

signal.title: S&P/ASX 200
signal.standing: The 200 largest companies listed on the Australian Securities Exchange in Sydney, weighted by market value. Miners and banks dominate it, and it is often the first major market to react to Chinese demand data.

signal.title: FTSE MIB
signal.standing: The FTSE MIB tracks the 40 largest, most traded companies on Borsa Italiana in Milan, Italy's main market. Banks and utilities dominate it, and it is the market most sensitive to Italian sovereign debt spreads.

signal.title: SSE Composite
signal.standing: Mainland China's main board, in Shanghai, tracking every A- and B-share listed there — state banks, insurers and industrial groups by weight. Largely closed to foreign investors, so it follows domestic policy more than global risk appetite.

signal.title: IDX Composite
signal.standing: Every company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in Jakarta, weighted by size. It is the market of the world's largest Muslim-majority country, and banks and commodity producers carry most of its weight.

signal.title: MERVAL
signal.standing: The Merval tracks the most traded shares on Argentina's exchange in Buenos Aires. It is priced in pesos, which have repeatedly lost most of their value, so it rises even in bad years; only a day's direction means something.

signal.title: TAIEX
signal.standing: Every common stock listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange in Taipei, weighted by market value. TSMC alone is roughly a third of the index, which makes it the most concentrated major market on the map.

signal.title: NASDAQ-100
signal.standing: The 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange in the United States, weighted by market value. A handful of technology giants make up most of it, so it works as a gauge of what investors pay for big tech.

signal.title: SENSEX
signal.standing: The Sensitive Index: 30 large, heavily traded companies on the Bombay Stock Exchange in Mumbai, India. The exchange, founded in 1875, is Asia's oldest, and the index is the benchmark for Indian equities.

signal.title: Nikkei 225
signal.standing: The Nikkei 225 tracks 225 large companies on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, Japan's main market, weighted by share price. It is Asia's largest exchange and the first major market to price each trading day.

signal.title: FTSE/JSE All Share
signal.standing: The FTSE/JSE All Share Index covers nearly all the market value listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange in South Africa. It is Africa's largest exchange by far, and the continent's only one with a usable public daily series.

signal.title: FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI
signal.standing: The Kuala Lumpur Composite Index tracks the 30 largest companies on Bursa Malaysia, the national stock exchange. The exchange is the world's largest market for Islamic finance instruments and the centre of the global sukuk trade.

signal.title: IBEX 35
signal.standing: The 35 most liquid companies on the Bolsa de Madrid, Spain's main stock market. Banks with heavy Latin American exposure carry much of its weight, which makes it a proxy for both regions.

signal.title: Straits Times Index
signal.standing: The Straits Times Index tracks the 30 largest companies listed on the Singapore Exchange, Southeast Asia's financial hub. Three local banks carry much of its weight, alongside regional property groups.

validated.text: Brazilian stocks on São Paulo's B3 exchange climbed 9.6% across five sessions that spanned Sunday's first-round presidential election, in which Flávio Bolsonaro beat Lula 47% to 45.1%. The run also overlapped with the Banco Master collapse, which cost the deposit insurer $7.7bn. The coverage does not tie the rise to either event.

Israeli stocks on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange fell 3.7% across five straight sessions to 7 October. The slide ran alongside coverage of a CIA report, carried by Drop Site, warning Israel risks civil war, and of Iran's proposed Hormuz ship ban reported by TASS. None of that coverage ties these events to the market's decline.

Canadian stocks on the Toronto Stock Exchange fell 3.1% over 4 straight sessions from 2026-09-03 to 2026-09-10. The slide overlapped with a trade fight with the US: Washington banned Canadian dairy, alcohol and motorcycles outright, and Canada's $20 billion in counter-tariffs took effect Tuesday. No report here links the drop to either step.

Stocks on the Taiwan Stock Exchange in Taipei rose 4.9% over 4 straight sessions, from 2026-09-15 to 2026-09-21. The only related coverage in that window was a 2026-09-16 story on Lithuania's lasers guarding Taiwan's chips. It is about chip-supply security, and nothing supplied connects it to the rise.

Big American tech stocks on the Nasdaq in the United States gained 5.3% over 5 sessions to 2026-09-23. News that week about the giants that dominate the index included Microsoft's plan for $10 billion-plus across 4 Gulf states by 2030 and Nvidia's AI push in the United Arab Emirates. None of that coverage links these stories to the rise.

South African stocks on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange fell 4.3% over 5 sessions to 2026-09-30. The slide ran alongside a rough stretch of news: US sanctions that Pretoria disputes, and a Durban terminal handling 30% less cargo after a software switch. The coverage does not tie these events to the fall.

Shares on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange fell 2.6% in one session to 2 October. The drop coincided with friction involving China: it demanded copper guarantees for the Anglo Teck merger, MI5 said 100+ UK academics joined Chinese-funded projects, and the Philippines said it forced a Chinese survey ship from Batanes. The coverage ties none to the fall.

Indian stocks on the Bombay Stock Exchange fell 2.7% across 4 straight sessions to 1 October. The slide ran alongside trade friction with Washington: the US Trade Representative said an India deal is not imminent, and Modi and Trump spoke amid a Russian-oil sanctions threat. India's monsoon also ended 12.6% below the long-term average.
